title: How a level of my pixel art tower defense gets made: blockout → Nano Banana → scripts → Godot
author: maskfallgame
selftext:
This is how the first level of Maskfall (a pixel art tower defense for iPhone and Android, made in Godot) goes from idea to game. Small studio (solo) in Italy, alongside my day job.

First of all the idea, the reference images, the palette, the story etc.

Then:

**1. Blockout.** A script draws the level layout in flat colors: road, tower slots, river, buildings. Why: at first I gave Nano Banana a simple plan and it moved the roads and invented extra slots. A flat-color blockout plus "repaint this" keeps the measures.

**2. Nano Banana.** It repaints the blockout, with the first level's concept (the one I picked) as style reference and a small catalogue of our buildings. Also, a palette of colours is helpful.

**3. Our scripts.** They reduce each background to its own 64-color palette, cut out what stands up (houses, trees, the mill) so units walk behind it, bake the shadows and build the layers the game needs.

**4. Characters and towers.** Concept from Nano Banana, then PixelLab for sprites, poses and directions, then the same scripts clean palette, outlines and frames.

**5. Code.** Claude Code writes the game in Godot. Bots play the levels to help with balancing.

What didn't work:
- At first all the art was drawn with code only (8 rounds on the same bridge). Then I moved to generators.
- Assembling assets generated one by one looked off. One whole background generated at once works much better.

One question for you: how do you keep a consistent style across 17+ generated backgrounds?

Thanks for any suggestions.

comments.author: maskfallgame
comments.body: Thanks! Fair point. The river is straight because it came straight from the blockout (no gameplay reason, the road just has to cross it on the bridge). Other levels have more natural water (a ford, a dry riverbed on the coast), but I'll try a version of this one with some curves

comments.author: maskfallgame
comments.body: Thanks, that's close to what we do: a style guide, the first level's concept as the target, and a catalogue of our buildings attached to every prompt. The hardest part is keeping light and colors the same from level to level (each background gets its own palette after the reduction). Do you use one shared palette for all your maps?

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body:
I learned that for consistency it helps to generate everything in one go.

So don't open a chat and make one art. Then another chat for another art. But one chat and say: one at a time make the arts. This keeps "the same mind" working on all of them. 

That said, why do all your maps need the same lighting? Different biomes have different lighting.

replies.author: maskfallgame
replies.body: I'll try to keep consistency by using one chat. You're right about lighting: the mountains and the coast already have different lighting. What I try to keep consistent is within one area, so the levels in the same chapter look like they're in the same place.

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body:
So make all scenes in the same area in the same chat. And other biomes in other chats. Otherwise they influence eachother too.

Also lighting comes from.. actual lights, and post processing. I feel we can get away with a lot by using strong post processing for example on a rainy map.

replies.author: maskfallgame
replies.body:
Makes sense, one chat per area then. Thanks!

And yes on post processing: one level has a leaden, stormy sky and most of that mood comes from grading after the palette reduction, not from the generation itself.

comments.author: StandardCategory5153
comments.body: It still looks very "ai pixel art" it has no soul/style. That's your biggest problem. There's 1000s of pixel art games that look like this.

replies.author: maskfallgame
replies.body:
Fair, and thanks for being direct. The background is the calmest part on purpose (it has to stay readable under the action), but I get that from this image alone it looks generic.

Honest question: what would make it stand out for you? A stronger palette, more personality in the units, something else?

replies.author: StandardCategory5153
replies.body:
Yes, I'm a professional game dev. I totally understand readability. That's not the issue.

IMO technically there's major things wrong with the screenshots.

* The perspectives are all off. The houses vs the bridge. etc.
* The detail quality is all over the place, the house detail vs like the roads. It's not consistent.
* Lastly, shadows are not logical. You have bright rocks under trees. etc. And you have different directions of shadows from 1 light source (the sun). it makes no sense.

It's clear to me you're not a trained artist. But that's ok! You can train and learn and fix that very easily by understanding the issues and prompting them to be fixed!

Now -- From a non-technical perspective the issue is it looks like every other AI pixel art fantasy game. That's due to your stylization choices, your palette, your line thickness, your propoprtions. You can fix all that too!

I'd go find references to other games or art styles you like and start experimenting! Also It looks like its WW2 focused? So you can really lean into WW2 art styles with the lore of your game (is it brutal? is is cartoony? Is it dark? Is it casual?)

Right now you just prompted "make ww2 buildings and soldiers and landscapes" That's not really art because art is about a highly focused vision. AI can do that for you! But you need to add the human into it.

replies.author: maskfallgame
replies.body:
This is really useful, thank you for taking the time. You're right, I'm not a trained artist, and that's exactly the kind of feedback I can't get on my own.

I'll go back to test with your list: one light direction for all shadows, one point of view for houses and bridge, same level of detail between buildings and roads. And I'll work on a more focused style (palette, line thickness, proportions, etc).

Small note on the setting: it's not WW2 exactly, it's an alternate 1940s Europe where the world wars never happened (the enemy is a masked army with red-lens gas masks and weird machines). That's probably something I need to show better too.

comments.author: Left-Excitement3829
comments.body: I like the blockout more tbh. ! V cool tho
